[MUJAHID:v2p504#4/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · أبو العالية | reports | Commanding right and forbidding wrong means calling people to faith and forbidding worship of idols.
[MUQATIL:31:16-18/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Luqman commands prayer, enjoining monotheism and forbidding evil, and patience through injury in this work; enduring it is among the firm obligations God imposed.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p676/r3] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · السدي | reports | Prayer and commanding right mean calling to monotheism; forbidding wrong means forbidding shirk. Abu al-ʿAliya similarly says commanding God’s worship and forbidding idols fulfills the command.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p676/r4] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The resolved matters include patience through affliction; the source glosses resolve as decisively cutting something off.
[TAB-FULL:v18p558/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Luqman tells his son to perform prayer with its prescribed bounds, command people to obey God, forbid disobedience and prohibited acts, and patiently endure harm caused by this duty without being deterred.
[TAB-FULL:v18p558/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | These duties are among the matters God firmly commanded; Ibn Jurayj likewise glosses them as matters God decisively enjoined.
[NAHHAS:v3p285/r8] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Establishing prayer means completing all its obligations and fulfilling every right of the entrusted work.
[NAHHAS:v3p285/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Patience with hardship means not moving from grief into disobedience; it also means patience against sins.
[SULAMI:v2p131/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Divine commands include obligation, creation, transformation, threat, guidance, decree, mockery, customary practice, public duty, benevolence, and sufficiency, each illustrated by a Quranic command. | mentions 2:43, 2:117, 7:166, 41:40, 4:135, 17:23, 17:64, 33:53, 9:71, 58:11, 9:5
[SULAMI:v2p131/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Luqman tells his son to pray, enjoin good, forbid wrong, begin with himself, and patiently endure trials, which turn into gifts.
[SULAMI:v2p131/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Patience is ceasing to complain about sudden trials while staying alert when sudden blessings arrive.
[THALABI:v7p314/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The resolute matters are obligations God commanded.
[THALABI:v7p314/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas glosses it as matters of resolve.
[THALABI:v7p314/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil glosses it as matters that are right.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p337/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | عزم الأمور may mean God's commanded matters, matters firmly controlled, or matters decisively settled; resolve and caution may be synonyms or differ.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p337/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | If resolve and caution differ, caution is either watchfulness while resolve is strength, or preparation while resolve is carrying through; a proverb warns against resolve without caution.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p337/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | A second proverb distinguishes preparing carefully from resolving and acting once the way is clear.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v4p337/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Patience is required either for harm suffered while commanding right and forbidding wrong or for trials in one's person or property.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p18/r4] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The strongest way to command good is to practice what one urges and refrain from what one forbids; one who cannot govern himself cannot govern others.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p18/r5] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | The good to be commanded is whatever brings a servant to God, and the evil to be forbidden is whatever distracts the servant from God.
[QUSHAYRI:v3p18/r6] QUSHAYRI, d. 465 · author | holds | A person who stands for God’s right will be tested and must patiently endure for God; whoever is patient for God does not lose by God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس ومقاتل | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil take enjoining right as faith in God and monotheism; another interpretation is obedience to God and following His command.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the evil to forbid is shirk, described as a wrong against oneself.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil interprets the evil as hidden or unrecognized shirk.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī explains the command as denouncing injustice and making justice manifest; another view takes evil as disobedience to God.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس ومقاتل | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say to endure the harm encountered in obedience to God through commanding right and forbidding wrong.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says resolute affairs means the reality of faith.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqātil interprets the resolute affairs as patience in enduring harm, a duty God commanded.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Al-Kalbī refers the phrase to commanding right and forbidding wrong; the author prefers it to encompass the commands, prohibitions, and patience together. | mentions 2:68
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p111/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The verse establishes the duty to command right, forbid wrong, and endure hardship; fear of harm should not stop the duty unless the feared harm is beyond one’s ability to bear.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:31:17-22/r1] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | Resolving to do what is right is among the obligatory matters.
[DAMGHANI:v1p325/r1] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | ʿAzm means firm resolve and firmness.
[JISHUMI:v8p5649/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حفص عن عاصم | reports | Ḥafṣ opens the yāʾ of “my son” throughout the Qur'an; the other readers use kasra. Sukun follows the original form, fatḥa drops the possessive after three yāʾs, and kasra is close to the possessive form.
[JISHUMI:v8p5653/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | ʿAzm is firm commitment and preparing oneself to do something; fakhara is recounting one's merits, while ikhtiyāl is swaggering pride.
[JISHUMI:v8p5658/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The command to enjoin right and forbid wrong also entails patience with the harm encountered in doing so.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p289/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The command to endure concerns harm suffered while enjoining good and forbidding wrong; these duties and patience under their harm are obligatory matters or matters one must resolve to fulfill.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p289/r14] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · وهب | reports | Wahb says Luqman articulated twelve thousand branches of wisdom that people incorporated into their sayings, judgments, and maxims.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p289/r15] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · خالد الربعي | reports | Khalid al-Rabi recounts that Luqman's master asked for the best and then worst two morsels; both times Luqman brought the tongue and heart, good or bad according to their condition.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r12] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · نافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وأبو بكر عن عاصم | reports | These readers double the yāʾ and give it kasra in the three occurrences of yā bunayya; Hafs and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿAsim double it with fatḥa.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p347#2/r13] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · ابن أبي برة عن ابن كثير وقنبل | reports | Ibn Abi Barra reports Ibn Kathir with a silent yāʾ in the first occurrence, kasra in the second, and fatḥa in the third; Qunbul reports silence in the first and third and kasra in the second.
[TABRISI:31:16-18/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Establish the obligatory prayer in its proper time and with its conditions; command obedience as right and forbid every rationally or legally vile act as wrong.
[TABRISI:31:16-18/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · علي | reports | Patience here means enduring hardship and injury incurred while commanding right and forbidding wrong.
[TABRISI:31:16-18/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · الجبائي | reports | Alternatively, patience concerns worldly hardships and misfortunes such as illness.
[TABRISI:31:16-18/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | ʿAzm al-umūr may mean sound resolve to do good rather than evil, a firm prior intention; wavering contradicts resolve, and other accounts gloss it as steadfastness or strength and caution.
[TABRISI:31:16-18/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The repeated diminutive bunayya expresses tenderness and compassion, not contempt.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p574/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أهل التفسير | reports | Maʿruf means monotheism in the command to enjoin it in 9:71 and 31:17; the source also groups 9:112. | mentions 9:112
[RAZI-FULL:v25p130#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After forbidding shirk and recalling God’s knowledge and power, Luqman commands prayer as sincere worship; prayer existed in earlier religious communities, though its form differed.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p130#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One who worships God completes himself; enjoining right and forbidding wrong helps complete others, the work of prophets and their learned successors.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p130#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The order differs from the earlier counsel because Luqman assumed his son already acknowledged God’s existence and therefore first needed prohibition of shirk; commentators report that the son was a polytheist whom Luqman continued to admonish until he accepted Islam.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p130#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Those who enjoin right and forbid wrong will be harmed, so Luqman tells his son to endure what befalls him.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p130#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Among the resolute matters” means obligatory and firmly determined; t

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p415/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المبرد | rejects | Abu Hayyan rejects al-Mubarrad’s claim that the initial consonant changed between ʿazm and ḥazm, since each word has its own complete derivation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p415/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Luqman orders prayer first as the noblest act of turning toward God, then enjoining good and forbidding wrong, then enduring hardship.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p415/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Patience covers all calamities, especially harm caused by enjoining right and forbidding wrong; the adviser should first embody what he teaches.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p415/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “That” refers to all the preceding commands and prohibitions; “resolute matters” may mean matters resolved upon or matters that are themselves resolute.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p415/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj explains these as things God has resolved and commanded.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p338/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Patience through people's harm is one of the resolute affairs.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p340/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · لقمان | reports | Luqman illustrates the force of his advice by taking one mustard seed from a bag with each admonition until the bag is empty; the mountain would have split from the counsel, and his son did so.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p340/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet names Luqman, the Negus, and Bilal among three distinguished Black figures; al-Ṭabarānī explains that Abyssinians are meant.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p341/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أنس | reports | A report says a poor man in two worn garments may pass unrecognized at people's doors, yet if he swears by God, God fulfills his oath.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p341/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أنس | reports | A report calls the pious wealthy who are unnoticed when present and unmissed when absent lamps purified from every dark, disgraceful trial.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p341/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عبد الله بن مسعود | reports | The Prophet says an unregarded man in worn clothes may have his oath fulfilled by God; if he asks for Paradise, God gives it, though He gives him nothing of worldly status.
